The decomposition into "product improvement vs segmentation artifact vs bad instrumentation" is the right shape, but I'd sharpen it: those aren't three separate hypotheses, they're nested, and instrumentation is upstream of the other two. Specifically — "seat expansion hides the drop" isn't a segmentation artifact. It's a measurement-definition problem. You're aggregating seats (which expand on annual renewal) over users (who churn). Stripe says "account is alive." App events say "this user logged in this month." If you've been reporting the first as retention, you've been hiding the second.

So the diagnostic isn't "pull raw cuts and stare." It's: pull three cuts of the same cohort, defined three ways, and see where they diverge.

1. Account-active (Stripe billing state) — what the current chart is.
2. User-active (app events, per-seat or per-active-user).
3. Logo-active (paid through month X, regardless of seat count).

If 1 and 3 stay flat past month 4 but 2 drops, that's the seat-hides-user-churn story. Defensible in the room: "here's what we measure, here's why this is the real signal, here's the per-seat trend we track alongside."

If 1 and 2 look the same but 3 drops, that's the more dangerous one — paying customers not using the product. Different conversation, different slide.

If all three drop together, it's product, and you have to be honest about what month 4 represents. Some teams don't need more monthly once their integration is done — that might be fine, but you have to say it that way.

On "tonight" — I'd actually push back on pulling raw cuts without a hypothesis to test. Cutting cohort data ad-hoc when you've already decided the number is wrong is how you produce a slide you're embarrassed by in 48 hours. The hour of work that helps is defining the three cuts and the join logic on paper — no Stripe or app access needed. That part is a pencil sketch of "what counts as retained." Then run the cuts tomorrow morning with fresh eyes.

The honest room answer is probably one of these two:

"We had a measurement-definition problem — we were reporting account-active as retention, which hid user-level churn we already see in the data. Here's the corrected cut and the plan to make it the source of truth."

or

Real decision matrix: trajectory vs. tier-jump. If 500k MAU is plausibly 12-18 months out, Clerk's DX wins and migrating later is cheap. If you'll be there in 6 months, Auth0's config-sprawl tax is smaller than a surprise Clerk bump with revenue already signed.

While you sit: pin down which Auth0 pain is actually driving it — feature surface, or operational sprawl. Clerk has less sprawl but isn't zero, so if sprawl is the real complaint, that's the tiebreaker.

Clerk
- What it is: managed auth service with drop-in React/Next UI, hosted user mgmt, social logins + MFA baked in.
- Upsides: fastest path to shipping, polished prebuilt components, orgs/SSO ready without engineering work.
- Biggest worry: pricing turns ugly past ~500k MAU and the user data model locks you in.

Auth0
- What it is: mature identity platform, broad protocol support, enterprise-grade reliability and compliance posture.
- Upsides: rock-solid uptime, huge integration catalog, clear paths to SOC2 / HIPAA / FedRAMP.
- Biggest worry: gets expensive fast and the dashboard/config UX is heavy for a small team.

Custom auth
- What it is: hand-rolled auth using Lucia, Auth.js, or your own JWT/session logic against your own DB.
- Upsides: full control, no per-MAU fees, no vendor lock-in, user data stays in-house.
- Biggest worry: you own the whole security surface — resets, sessions, MFA, breach response, audits.

1. Bump the basic-auth tier on whatever's sitting behind v1.
   - What it is: pay for a higher req/min cap on the current provider and keep the existing setup as-is.
   - Upside: immediate, no customer-visible change, no rewrite window, no migration risk during a traffic-up period.
   - Biggest worry: still basic auth — next traffic bump hits the same wall again; you're buying headroom, not changing the ceiling.

2. Decouple POST /v1/webhooks (the one you added Apr 8) from basic auth before paying for a tier bump.
   - What it is: move inbound webhook verification to HMAC or a per-endpoint secret so webhook traffic stops sharing the same auth bucket as the rest of v1.
   - Upside: pulls the noisiest contributor out — bigger accounts with webhooks retrying are probably most of the new pressure; the rest of v1 gets a lot of headroom back for free, and the tier you do buy goes further.
   - Biggest worry: now you're running two auth schemes on v1; if the Clerk/Auth0 rewrite lands later, this is one more thing to migrate.

3. Use the cap pressure as the forcing function to commit on the Clerk vs Auth0 decision you were still weighing on Apr 9.
   - What it is: pick one and start the rewrite now, instead of waiting for the next bump and having this conversation again.
   - Upside: ends the recurring "is this intermittent" cycle permanently; gets you off basic auth entirely before the tier math stops working.
   - Biggest worry: rewriting auth while traffic is spiking is the worst window, and the Auth0 cost-creep concern you flagged is still unresolved.

The shape you want: acknowledge → redirect to the framework → set real timing → close without committing to outcome. The whole point is to make Jake feel heard while keeping the decision located outside the room.

1.  Open with the act, not the substance. "Thanks for putting this on the 1:1 agenda directly." You're validating that he raised it the right way — not that his read is correct, and not that you'll fix it.

2.  Move the decision off your shoulders. "Comp moves through [leveling review / annual cycle / calibration]." The first time you say "the process" instead of "I," the room changes. Now it's the framework vs. his ask, not you vs. him.

3.  Make the process concrete. Name the inputs, the reviewers, the months. Vague process sounds like "Morgan will decide"; specific process sounds like a system. Specificity here is your friend.

4.  Commit only to the framework step. "I'll make sure your case is in front of the right inputs" — not "I'll take care of it," not "let me see what I can do." Those phrasings put discretion back in your hands, which is exactly what you don't want.

5.  Things to not say, even as filler: "you're right," "you should be paid more," any number, any percentage, an arbitrary "let's revisit in Q3" that isn't the actual cycle, or escalating to the board without a process trigger. Each of those creates an implied promise that lives outside the framework.

If he pushes for a read in the moment, the cleanest move is "I'd be guessing — the framework is what I trust on this, not my gut." Keeps it warm but bounded.

- A short list of states that are legible on first read to an external user.

5) Evidence that earns try-with-real-workflow confidence
- A clean first-run path end to end.

- Proof that invited-member / admin handoff is not brittle.
- A clear separation between sample/preview data and real activated state.

Total: 12:00 | Format: prepared remarks + collected-Q answers only, no live Q&A


[0:00 – 0:45]  INTRO  (45 sec)

Cue: stand, acknowledge, settle the room.

Open with HR's suggested line verbatim:

[0:45 – 4:30]  MERCURY — BOUNDED TESTING  (3 min 45 sec)

Lead line: "Mercury is in bounded testing. That's the operating frame for everything I'm about to say."

1. What "bounded" means in practice.
   - Design partners only. No general availability.
   - They connect to preview data, not live production sources. Deliberate scope choice — we want to learn the workspace/sync plumbing under real usage before we touch live data contracts.
   - Named cohort. Don't name them in this room; the operating fact is bounded cohort, not a public beta.

2. Why bounded, not bigger.
   - Mercury is the plumbing layer underneath the whole product. If we ship it leaky, we spend Q4 cleaning up customer trust instead of hardening the product.
   - Bounded = real usage signal (what breaks, what feels slow, what customers expect that we haven't built) without a public blast radius.
   - This is an operating call. Not a launch-timing announcement.

3. What we're learning from it.
   - The Mercury signal we want by end of Q3 is operational: connector reliability, onboarding conversion, preview-data semantics.
   - That signal feeds Q4 hardening priorities. It is not packaged for outside the building.

Transition: "So that's Mercury — bounded, deliberate, and the input to Q4 planning. Which is the next block."


[4:30 – 7:30]  Q4 HARDENING PRIORITIES  (3 min)

Lead line: "Q4 is a hardening quarter. Let me be specific about what that means and what it doesn't mean."

1. What hardening actually covers.
   - Reliability and correctness on the Mercury plumbing that design partners are exercising today.
   - Onboarding follow-through — the path from a new workspace to a first useful sync. This is where activation lives, so this is where we focus.
   - The launch-blocker bar: a Mercury issue that affects customer trust, data correctness, or workspace stability is a launch blocker. Anything that improves feel or scope but the contract holds is a follow-up item.

2. What hardening does NOT mean.
   - Not a feature freeze. If a scoped bet fits inside a team's existing capacity without crowding out hardening, it can ship.
   - Not a slowdown on hiring. Hiring stays on the same plan.
   - Not a signal we're pulling back from product ambition. It is a higher bar on what ships before we add more surface area.

3. How we decide blocker vs follow-up.
   - Three-question test on every Mercury issue:
     - Does it break a customer's data, contract, or trust? → blocker.
     - Does it slow them down but the contract holds? → follow-up.
     - Is it a feature ask masquerading as a bug? → roadmap, not hardening.

Transition: "Hardening is the operating frame. The next piece is a concrete example of what good looks like inside that frame — Jordan's Honeycomb debugging write-up."


[7:30 – 9:00]  JORDAN'S HONEYCOMB EXAMPLE  (1 min 30 sec)

Lead line: "I'm calling this out at all-hands because it's the kind of debugging habit I want to see across the company, not just in one incident."

1. What it was, in one line.
   - A Mercury-side latency incident that crossed three services and two teams. Jordan wrote it up in Honeycomb with the trace, the hypothesis tree, and the resolution — and shared it before the incident channel went cold.

2. Why it matters more than the bug itself.
   - Not the tool. Honeycomb is useful; that's not the point.
   - Not just the debugging skill. Plenty of people debug well in private.
   - The cross-team loop — the write-up landed in front of the people who needed to see it while the context was still live. That part is worth scaling.

3. What we're taking from it.
   - For incidents that touch more than one team: a short Honeycomb write-up within 24 hours of resolution. Not a postmortem deck — a trace + hypothesis tree + what we changed.
   - Eng leadership will publish a lightweight template next week. Expectation, not policy.

SECTION 1 — ACTIVATION SPLIT FOR OCTOBER: 19/27 vs 16/27
Owner: Anna. This is the headline number Sofia is pressing on.

  - Restate the corrected activation definition (single source of truth):
    An account is "activated within 7 days" when EITHER
      (a) `real_source_connected` fires within 7 days of workspace creation, OR
      (b) `first_live_sync_completed` fires within 7 days of workspace creation.
    The two events are deduplicated. Do not add them.

  - October numbers, plain English:
      27 accounts entered the bounded flow.
      19/27 activated within 7 days (the OR-union, deduplicated) = 70%.
      16/27 completed first live sync within 7 days = 59%.
      The 3-account gap (19 - 16) is the "real-source connected but not first-live-sync" cohort.

  - What the gap is and is not:
      IS: accounts that connected a real source in week 1 and did not finish a successful live sync in that window.
      IS NOT: a separate funnel stage we are hiding; not a failure mode by definition.
      IS NOT: double-counted in 19/27; the dedup rule protects this.

  - Where the lift comes from (the honest read):
      Real-source connection is a lower bar than first live sync. Source connect can happen in minutes (admin clicks through, repo/token attaches). First live sync depends on the source being healthy, permissions being right end-to-end, and the destination accepting the payload.
      So the 3 accounts in the gap are typically "source attached, sync still pending or in retry" — neither stalled nor failed, just not yet through the live-sync gate by day 7. Some of them sync by day 10–14 and show up in the first-live-sync cohort on a relaxed window; some stay in retry/permissions limbo and become the slower-ramp cohort in section 3.

SECTION 2 — WHAT COUNTS, WHAT DOES NOT, WHERE LIFT COMES FROM
Owner: Anna.

  - Counts as activation in 7 days:
      - `real_source_connected` event fires within 7 days of workspace creation, OR
      - `first_live_sync_completed` event fires within 7 days of workspace creation.
      - Deduplicated against the other event for the same account.

  - Does NOT count as activation:
      - Workspace created with no source attached.
      - Teammate invited but no source connection by day 7.
      - Demo / sample / sandbox source only (no real source).
      - API key generated but no source connected.
      - Source connection attempted and failed, with no successful retry by day 7.

  - Where the lift in 19/27 vs 16/27 comes from, in pattern terms:
      - Source connect is admin-side and one-click-ish in most bounded-flow paths.
      - First live sync is system-side and waits on permissions, source health, and downstream acceptance.
      - The 3-account lift is the wedge where admin action outruns system outcome. It is not a product win we should market; it is a tail we should explain.

SECTION 3 — UNEVEN EXPANSION IN PATTERN TERMS
Owner: Anna. This is the section Sofia asked about as "where accounts fail to expand cleanly after activation." Map every failure mode we have evidence for; mark the ones we do not yet have evidence for as open.

      Mechanism: admin hit the connect/import/continue decision and bounced. Owner question: was this a permissions wall, a confusing handoff state, or just deprioritized?

  - Pattern B — Slower usage ramp after first sync:
      Symptom: first live sync completed, but usage (queries, syncs, downstream consumers) stays flat for 2–4 weeks.
      Mechanism: sync worked once; team has not yet wired Scaffold into a recurring workflow. Not a failure — just slow expansion.
      Evidence base: Q3 cohort read from 2023-11-17. This is the cohort the hybrid pricing model is built to handle (section 4).

SECTION 4 — HYBRID PRICING LOGIC: WHY MAU IS THE HONEST RAMP MEASURE
Owner: Devon. This is Devon's section.

  - The setup we are defending:
      Mercury pricing is hybrid: a usage-ramp core measured in MAU (monthly active developer usage), with a seat floor and explicit usage overage bands surfaced as a comparison column even where it is not the recommended path.

  - Why MAU is the honest ramp measure:
      - It tracks actual adoption — whether developers are running syncs, queries, and downstream consumers in a given month.
      - It rewards expansion that produces usage and discounts expansion that is seat-only (directory inflation, dormant accounts, shared mailboxes, license hoarding).
      - It is the only metric that survives the uneven-expansion patterns in section 3. A seat or directory metric would bill Pattern B (slow ramp after first sync) as if usage had happened, and would not bill Pattern D (trust stall) as the constraint it actually is.

  - Why not purchased seats:
      - Purchased seats are a procurement convenience, not an adoption signal. A customer can buy 50 seats and have 6 active. The seat number would overstate both footprint and value, and we would have to renegotiate every time usage and license diverge.
      - Seat-only pricing reintroduces the overpricing problem on the ramp-up path that hybrid pricing was built to avoid. Seat floor must stay below full directory.

  - Why not directory size:
      - Directory size includes contractors, alumni, shared mailboxes, and bot accounts that will never log into Scaffold. It is the worst of the three on honesty and the best on procurement framing — which is why we keep it out of the price logic even when procurement teams ask for it.
      - Mercury procurement framing: budget figures stay budgetary guidance; no enterprise SSO/audit/admin line item or customer-specific carve-outs in the procurement packet.

  - How to think about accounts that activate but expand slowly (Pattern B):
      - Under MAU, they pay for what they use, not for what they intended to use.
      - Under seat, they would pay for the intended footprint and resent it.
      - Under directory, they would pay for org-chart size and resent it harder.
      - The hybrid floor exists so a slow-expansion account has a known minimum we can forecast against, and a known ceiling they can plan into — neither of which a pure-MAU model gives Devon for procurement conversations.

  - Internal note (not for Sofia, not for procurement):

5. How do you tell the difference between "the customer needs to be educated on what already exists" and "we genuinely don't have this and promising it would be a mistake"? Give me a recent example of each call.
6. Our roadmap has hard limits on what can be promised externally. Describe how you would work with product and engineering to set customer expectations without over-promising or losing the deal.

Working without a mature sales org
7. Walk me through a quarter where you were the first or only senior commercial person. Who prospected, who qualified, who drove expansion, and where did you spend your own time?
8. Assume no SDR, marketing ops, SE, or CSM for the next two quarters. What is the first motion you build, and what do you explicitly defer?

**Draft answers (technical, scoped to current API v2 quickstart / supported connector-auth model):**

1) **Cursor stability across auth-failed retries.** Cursor values returned by API v2 GraphQL connections are stable for replay within the lifetime of the connection — a transient auth failure on a page request does not invalidate the cursor. Replay the same `endCursor` from your last successful page. Restart-from-prior-page is only required if the connection itself expires or you receive a `PAGINATION_RESET` / similar error. Don't reset on every retry.

2) **JWT expiration during a retry.** Treat JWT refresh and GraphQL operation replay as separate concerns. If the token expired mid-retry: obtain a fresh token from your credential source, then replay the same GraphQL operation with the same variables and the same cursor (if pagination) — do not start a brand-new logical request just because the credential changed. The operation is still retryable; only the credential needs replacing. Don't conflate 401 with a logical failure unless the replay itself fails.

3) **Workspace-scoped token rotation in place.** Workspace-scoped tokens issued under the current connector/auth model can be rotated in place via the standard rotate-credential path on the existing workspace — it does not require a full customer reconnect. What's still true, same as before: rotation is bound to the same workspace; rotated tokens still go out as the canonical headers (`X-Scaffold-Workspace` + `X-Scaffold-Signature`), case-insensitive on receive; and a full reconnect is only required if the *workspace* itself changes, not the token.

Subject: Year-end team note draft
From: Devon Hayes

Team —

As we wrap 2024, we keep coming back to how much hard, unglamorous work it took to turn enterprise learning into product that is clearer, more repeatable, and easier for customers to trust on day one. We made real progress on the parts of Scaffold that decide whether a customer gets set up quickly, connects their first source, sees a live sync, invites teammates, and feels like the product can support a serious deployment.

Project Mercury pulled a lot of that into focus, but this was never just one project or one team. Engineering, product, design, support, and everyone carrying customer context helped turn one-off setup work into something we can ship again and again. Atlas also got stronger in the ways that matter most once customers are live — better auth and verification, more usable webhook and connector behavior, clearer docs, faster first technical reads, and less thrash on the issues that used to bounce around.

The year-end numbers tell the same story, in shorthand:

- Setup got quicker: median time from workspace creation to first connected source fell from 2.4 days in Q1 to 0.9 days in Q4.
- Activation got stickier: new workspaces reaching a first live sync within 14 days rose from 41% to 63%, and teammate invitations on activated workspaces climbed from 28% to 47%.
- The Mercury flow got more reliable: workspace creation success moved from 93.8% to 97.9%; first-source connection completion, from 54% to 72%; first successful sync on connected workspaces, from 68% to 84%.
- Enterprise readiness moved with it: admin-role setup on new enterprise workspaces rose from 61% to 88%; median time to close high-priority Atlas issues dropped from 2.6 business days to 0.9; and the auth / webhook / connector docs refresh deflected 37% of repeat enterprise implementation questions in the second half.

More important than any of those numbers, people kept showing up for each other while we were changing the product under real customer pressure. That takes judgment, patience, and a lot of follow-through that rarely gets enough credit.

Thank you for sticking with the hard parts, for caring about the details customers actually feel, and for helping build a company that learns and gets better instead of just getting louder. We're proud of what this team shipped in 2024 — and excited for what we get to build from here.

Compass October — status implementation (strict, not punitive)

2. Freshness warning handling (Anna 9/2)
   - freshness_warning is metadata, not a status. It renders next to the row and propagates into the caveat field as a prefill, but never changes owner_action_status.
   - "done" requires: evidence_source present AND (caveat present OR freshness_warning=false). The caveat prefill is editable; owners are expected to read it, not just accept it.
   - "rejected" is a separate, explicit transition. Rejection reason must be one of {evidence_too_thin, wrong_account, prompt_type_mismatch, out_of_scope}. evidence_too_thin requires evidence_source to be null OR point at a seed example OR predate the owner action by >90 days. Anything else fails the transition.

3. Seed examples (Sarah 9/2)
   - Seed rows ship with a system flag seed_example=true. The flag is invisible in the default view but exposed on hover. evidence_source for seed rows is literally the string "seed_example", which the done transition refuses.
   - Owners see a one-line reminder on first session: "Seed examples show row shape, not readout evidence." Reminder lives in the owner tool (not docs), dismissible per session, not per row.

4. Owner-action capture (Jake lane)
   - Internal-only flag on the workbench. No toggle in the UI for external viewers. If a Compass share link is generated for a non-internal account, the share is blocked at create-time, not redacted after.
   - Mercury source-owner path: ws setup → teammate invite/src-owner → first src connect → first live sync. Each step is a discrete owner_action_status transition with its own evidence_source. A row that jumps straight to "first live sync" without intermediate evidence gets reset to in_progress, not accepted as done.
   - Out-of-scope items (custom admin policy, granular role editor, dept-perm lock, SSO change, Atlas/auth scope) are not addable as Compass rows in October. The prompt_type picker excludes them; they exist as held items elsewhere.

5. Status transitions and the blocked_waiting_customer_follow_up rule (Sep 29)
   - blocked_waiting_customer_follow_up is sticky. It only clears on an actual customer reply captured as evidence_source (call log, email reply, in-product reply). An owner nudge or Sarah nudge does not clear it — those are recorded as owner_action notes, not status transitions.
   - If the row has been blocked_waiting_customer_follow_up for >30 days, it auto-escalates to rejected with reason evidence_too_thin and a "stale customer follow-up" caveat. Owners can override within 7 days by attaching a dated owner_action note, which resets the timer.

6. What "strict enough" means here
   - Strict at the transition layer (schema, evidence_source non-null, caveat required, out-of-scope excluded, blocked_waiting only clears on real customer reply). Owners can't accidentally smuggle seed examples, undated re-engagements, or out-of-scope items into done.

7. What this does NOT do
   - It does not turn freshness_warning into an auto-reject. It just refuses the done transition without a caveat.

# Verifying Atlas webhook signatures

Every webhook Atlas sends to your endpoint carries a signature header so you can confirm it came from us and that it hasn't been replayed. This section replaces the earlier patch and walks through the four questions support has heard most often in December: how the signature is built, how timestamps work, how to handle secret rotation, and what test-mode events look like.

If you only need the algorithm: it's HMAC-SHA256 over the string `<timestamp>.<raw request body>`, with the result prefixed `v1=` in the header. The rest of this section explains what that means and where customers most often go wrong.

## Headers you'll receive

- `X-Scaffold-Signature: t=<unix_seconds>,v1=<hex_hmac>`
- `X-Atlas-Timestamp: <unix_seconds>` (same value as `t=`; provided for visibility — verify against `t=`)

Signing is header-only. If you see a signature claim anywhere other than the `X-Scaffold-Signature` header (query string, body field, alternate header), ignore it.

## How the signature is computed

```
signed_string = timestamp + "." + raw_request_body
signature     = HMAC_SHA256(webhook_signing_secret, signed_string).hexdigest()
```

Use the **raw, unparsed** request body. Parsing first (e.g., JSON-decoding) and then re-serializing produces a different byte sequence and a different signature. If your framework auto-parses, capture the body off the request stream before parsing.

Python:

```python
import hmac, hashlib, time

def verify(payload: bytes, header: str, secret: str, tolerance: int = 300) -> bool:
    parts = dict(p.split("=", 1) for p in header.split(","))
    ts = int(parts["t"])
    v1 = parts["v1"]
    expected = hmac.new(
        secret.encode(), f"{ts}.".encode() + payload, hashlib.sha256
    ).hexdigest()
    if not hmac.compare_digest(expected, v1):
        return False
    return abs(int(time.time()) - ts) <= tolerance
```

Node:

```js
const crypto = require('crypto');

function verify(payload, header, secret, toleranceSec = 300) {
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(header.split(',').map(p => p.split('=', 2)));
  const ts = parseInt(parts.t, 10);
  const v1 = parts.v1;
  const expected = crypto
    .createHmac('sha256', secret)
    .update(`${ts}.`).update(payload)
    .digest('hex');
  if (!crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected), Buffer.from(v1))) return false;
  return Math.abs(Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - ts) <= toleranceSec;
}
```

## Timestamp tolerance — what it is, what it isn't

The `t=` value lets you reject deliveries that are too old (or too far in the future) relative to your server clock. Atlas's default tolerance window is **5 minutes**; this is configurable per integration.

A few points support has been asked to clarify:

- **Tolerance is replay protection, not a trust extension.** A signature inside the tolerance window still has to match the HMAC. A signature outside the window is rejected even if the cryptographic match would have passed. The window exists so that, if signing material is ever exposed, a captured-and-replayed payload has a bounded usefulness — not so that recent-but-unverified requests can be accepted.
- **Don't widen the tolerance to "fix" failed verifications.** If your endpoint is rejecting valid Atlas deliveries, the cause is almost always clock skew or secret-rotation drift, not the window being too tight. Walk the checklist at the bottom of this section before adjusting.
- **Run NTP.** If you operate across regions, keep clocks in sync. Atlas compares `t=` against its own clock at send time and expects the same standard on receipt.

## Rotating webhook secrets

Atlas supports a short overlap window during rotation:

1. In the dashboard, generate a new signing secret. The previous secret remains valid for **24 hours** by default.
2. During that overlap, your verifier should accept a signature that matches **either** the current or the previous secret.
3. After the overlap window, only the new secret validates.

Suggested rotation cadence: at personnel change, on suspected exposure, or at least annually. Most rotation-related tickets in December came from verifiers that only check one secret and then drop every webhook for the first few minutes of a rollover — implement overlap-aware verification before you need it.

If you suspect an active exposure rather than a planned rotation, contact support to invalidate the previous secret out of band; this is typically handled within the same business day.

## Test-mode events

The dashboard's "Send test event" tool produces real signed webhooks so you can exercise your verification logic. Differences from live events:

- The payload includes `"test_mode": true`.
- Event types are namespaced under `test.*` (e.g., `test.connection.sync_completed`).
- The signature uses the same signing secret as live events for your integration.

Route test events to a sandbox handler, or branch on `test_mode` in your handler, so test deliveries can't accidentally trigger production side effects. Test events honor the same tolerance window as live events.

## If verification is still failing

Before opening a ticket, walk this list once — most December tickets resolved on items 1, 2, or 4:

1. Are you signing the **raw** body, or a re-serialized version?
2. Are you reading the secret from where you think you are (env var, secrets manager, dashboard copy)?
3. Are you using the integration's **current** secret, or did rotation happen recently without your verifier learning the previous one?
4. Is your server clock within 5 minutes of real time?
5. Does the URL on the dashboard match what Atlas is actually POSTing to (path, host, scheme)?

If you've checked all five and it's still failing, open a support ticket with:

- The full `X-Scaffold-Signature` header value from a failing delivery (timestamp + v1).
- The first ~200 bytes of the raw body, redacted if it contains customer data.
- Your endpoint URL and the UTC time you ran verification.
- Your tolerance window setting.
- The event ID, if your parser got far enough to extract one.

Support can almost always diagnose from those five items. Without them, the ticket typically has to round-trip.

## What this patch does not change

- **Delivery timing.** Webhooks are best-effort and may be delayed by seconds to minutes. Don't couple business logic to webhook arrival time — poll or back off as you would for any other unreliable channel.
- **Retry behavior.** Atlas's retry policy is unchanged. Verification failures are not retried; an unverifiable delivery is treated as undelivered.
- **Header contract.** Still `X-Scaffold-Signature` only. A `v2=` prefix is not yet in use; if you see one, please report it.

Here's the revised section incorporating Leo's notes:

---

## Webhook signing verification

Every webhook delivery includes an `x-scaffold-signature` header containing an HMAC-SHA256 signature of the base string `${x-scaffold-timestamp}.${raw_request_body}`, computed with your workspace's active webhook secret. To verify:

1. Read the raw request body bytes **before** JSON parsing — any re-serialization will produce a different signature.
2. Concatenate the value of `x-scaffold-timestamp` with `.` and the raw body.
3. Compute HMAC-SHA256 using your webhook secret and compare to `x-scaffold-signature` in constant time.

Replay protection. Reject events whose `x-scaffold-timestamp` differs from your server time by more than five minutes, unless your consumer has a known queueing delay that justifies a wider window. The timestamp is part of the signed base string, so a valid signature does not by itself prove freshness.

Secret rotation. When you rotate the workspace webhook secret, deliveries generated before rotation continue to verify against the previous secret for 24 hours. Both secrets are accepted during that overlap window so in-flight retries don't fail.

Test mode. Test-mode events use the same signing scheme. They carry `event_mode: "test"` in the payload body so your handler can branch on it. Signatures still verify normally; you do not need separate test secrets.

Delivery semantics. We retry failed deliveries for up to 24 hours. Delivery is at-least-once, not exactly-once — design handlers to be idempotent and keyed off the event `id`.

If verification fails: confirm the secret matches the active secret for the workspace, confirm you are signing the raw body bytes (not a parsed-and-re-serialized object), and confirm the timestamp header is included in the base string. For rotation-related failures, also check whether the event was generated before the rotation timestamp.

Subject: Re: Atlas JWT verification failure

Hi — thanks for the detail. A JWT verification failure on Atlas calls can come from a few different things, and the most common causes we see in support are:

  • Clock skew between your service and Atlas. The token's `iat` / `nbf` claims fall outside the window Atlas accepts. Worth checking the host's NTP / time sync first — this is the cause in a clear majority of cases we've handled recently.
  • A stale signing key on your side after a key rotation that didn't fully propagate to all your services or environments.
  • Less commonly: a signing-secret mismatch between what your service is using and the key registered for that workspace.

We haven't changed Atlas auth semantics — verification is checking the same fields as before. This isn't an Atlas platform incident.

**Rewritten customer-visible paragraph (Atlas docs / support guidance)**

If a request to Atlas fails JWT verification, the most common causes are on the customer side and can be checked without contacting Scaffold support. Work through these in order:

- **Clock skew between the issuer and Atlas.** JWT `iat` (issued-at), `nbf` (not-before), and `exp` (expiration) are evaluated against Atlas's server clock. If the system that mints your token is more than a minute or two ahead or behind Atlas, the token can be rejected as not-yet-valid, already-expired, or issued-in-the-future. Confirm the issuer host's time source (NTP) and compare it against a known-good reference.
- **Stale signing key after rotation.** When a workspace's signing key is rotated, previously issued tokens are no longer accepted. If verification recently started failing for tokens that were working, confirm that the verifying service is using the current key for that workspace and that any cached or pinned keys have been refreshed.
- **Signing-secret mismatch.** Atlas verifies the signature against the key registered for the workspace the token is being presented to. A token signed with the key from a different workspace, environment, or Atlas account will fail verification. Confirm the token's audience/workspace matches the key being used.
- **Other token-shape issues.** Make sure the token is a JWS in a format Atlas supports (for example, a signed JWT), that the header and payload are not truncated, and that the verifier is checking the signature against the raw token rather than a re-serialized copy.

These checks reflect how Atlas has always verified JWTs; there has been no change to Atlas authentication requirements. If verification still fails after reviewing the items above, share a redacted token (header and payload only, signature removed) along with the approximate request timestamp and the Atlas workspace or host, and support will assist.

PUBLISHABLE PARAGRAPH (Atlas JWT troubleshooting section)

If a Scaffold-issued JWT is rejected by your service, the cause is almost always one of four routine checks. First, verify clock skew: a token's `iat`, `nbf`, and `exp` are evaluated against your server's wall clock, and even a few minutes of drift between the issuer and the verifier will cause a valid-looking token to fail. Second, confirm the verifier is honoring all three of those claims — `iat` (issued-at), `nbf` (not-before), and `exp` (expiration) — rather than only `exp`, since omitting `nbf` or rejecting tokens whose `iat` is in the future is a common source of false negatives. Third, check that your service isn't pinning a stale signing key: keys are rotated on a published schedule, and tokens signed by a key your verifier still has cached past its retirement window will be rejected even if every claim is otherwise valid. Fourth, confirm the verifier is configured with the signing secret or JWKS endpoint that matches the workspace and environment you're testing against — a secret mismatch (for example, a staging secret used against production tokens, or a per-workspace secret left over from a prior workspace) produces the same generic "invalid signature" error. None of the above reflect a change in how Atlas issues tokens; they are the standard checks to run when any JWT integration stops working.

Ramp: yes. The hesitation is signal about the surface, not about him — wet apartment steps are the friction point. Use the ramp both directions today. If you don't have one for the building stairs yet, this is a reasonable week to order one; damp mornings will keep happening through spring.

Walk: flat pavement only, no curbs, no wet grass, no uphill. Cut it to roughly half your usual Lake Merritt loop — 15-20 minutes at his pace, not yours. Let him set the speed; if he trots comfortably the whole way you can extend slightly, if he slows or picks his feet up deliberately, turn around. The bar is "warm-up stiffness resolves within the first block or two and he moves normally after," not "zero hesitation anywhere." Some pickiness on slick spots is normal senior-dog behavior.

Move this from damp-step management to a vet call if you see any of:

- Limping or visibly off movement on flat ground (not just one obstacle)
- Stiffness that gets worse during the walk instead of loosening up
- Refusing to bear weight on a leg, or repeatedly lifting the same foot
- Yelping, flinching, or snapping when you touch his legs, paws, joints, or back
- Swelling, heat, or a visible wound on any paw or leg
- Refusing food or water, vomiting, or any unproductive retching/belly distension — bloat is always an emergency regardless of context
- Panting, shaking, or restlessness at home that doesn't settle within an hour
- Reluctance to move at all, or hiding/withdrawal past mid-morning
- The hesitation spreading to multiple obstacles — curbs he's handled fine before, getting on the couch, stairs inside the apartment

Single-step hesitation on a wet morning, in a dog who ate, is moving normally on flat ground, and is cheerful, reads as senior-dog caution, not injury. The moment the pattern broadens past the one friction point, that read changes.

Subject: Re: Department usage snapshot — overage resets & mid-quarter seat trades

Hi [Evergreen admin team],

Thanks for the reply — glad the preliminary department snapshot is useful. Two answers below.

1) When do the standard Growth overage increments reset?

Growth includes up to 200 monthly active developers (MAD) per billing month, with each additional 50-MAD band billed at $1,000. The "increment" is per 50-MAD band, and it resets every billing month — meaning usage is measured independently in each month, not accumulated across the quarter or year. If a department peaks above 200 MAD in March and then drops back under in April, March produces the overage band and April does not. Evergreen accepted this MAD accounting methodology in the January 20 redline, so what finance sees at month close is the same picture: one band at a time, billed monthly, no carry-forward.

2) Can departments trade seats mid-quarter to avoid overage?

There is no department-level seat cap or mid-quarter seat-trade carveout in the standard Growth subscription — the 200-MAD envelope is measured across the whole Evergreen workspace for the billing month, not allocated per department. In practice that means:

- If one department is quiet and another is busy, the active developers in the busy department still count toward the shared 200-MAD total for that month.
- Reassigning an internal "seat" from one department to another doesn't change the count, because the meter is real developer activity (API, dashboard, or write-sync activity during the month), not assigned license slots.
- Departments can absolutely coordinate internally — staggering rollouts, scheduling heavy sync windows in different weeks, or holding off on enabling a new team until a month where headroom exists — and that kind of operational planning is the right tool here.

If the department-by-department pattern in the preliminary CSV is sustained, the cleanest next step is a quick conversation about whether the overall Evergreen workspace is approaching a steady state above 200 MAD, which would be a sizing conversation for a future renewal rather than something we can solve inside the current quarter. Let me know if you'd like to set up that walkthrough, or if finance wants the final month-close numbers in any particular format.

Best,
Sarah

Hi {name},

Thanks for the detailed write-up — this matches an issue we've already corrected in the docs, not a verification-code defect. The Atlas API v2 JWT spec treats `nbf` as the literal instant a token becomes valid, and pasting the sample timestamp from the doc into a production token is the most common way to hit it: the moment your clock (or ours) skews past that hardcoded value, the token reads as not-yet-valid and starts failing intermittently.

A couple of things that will get you unblocked:

- Don't carry a fixed timestamp out of the sample. Set `nbf` (and `iat`) to the current time when you mint the token, or omit `nbf` entirely if you don't need a delayed-activation window.
- If you do set `nbf`, keep clock-skew tolerance in mind on both ends — a token minted for "now" can still look slightly future-dated to the server if your machine is ahead.
- The relevant section is "JWT claims → `nbf`" under Atlas API v2 Authentication in the docs (link: confirm the live page title before sending — search returned an index hit dated 2026-04-22 but no body).

If after that you're still seeing intermittent `nbf` rejections, send us: the request timestamp, the token's `nbf`/`iat` values, and a request id from a failing call — that gives us a concrete repro on the server side rather than guessing from the client.

Proposed redline for legal — drop-in draft, three clause-by-clause changes with a short note on each. Plain text below; legal can paste into a redline workbook.

---

Cover note for legal:

Below is our redline on the customer's three connector-related clauses. We've held the customer's support expectations (warranty is preserved as conformance to published docs; SLA credit structure stays; real deprecation notice + migration guidance) and removed the open-ended per-sync credit exposure and the per-customer change-control veto. The redline is consistent with our standard customer-side carveouts and the Atlas/API v2 support posture.

---

Clause 1 — Connector warranty

Customer's language:
  "Provider warrants that all listed source connectors are production-ready for Customer's use cases during the subscription term."

Proposed replacement:
  "Provider warrants that the Source Connectors made generally available to Customer (as listed in the Connector Documentation at [docs URL], as updated by Provider from time to time) will conform to the published Connector Documentation during the subscription term. Customer acknowledges that Connector behavior depends on (a) Customer's configuration of permissions, network access, and source-system credentials, and (b) the continued availability, API, schema, and terms of the third-party source system. Provider does not warrant that any Connector will operate with Customer's specific use case, source-system configuration, or data volume absent Provider's prior written approval of that use case."

Why: "Production-ready for Customer's use cases" is undefined and subjective — it expands the warranty into a per-integration fitness guarantee. Conformance-to-docs is the standard, bounded, objective warranty. The two-prong carveout (customer config + third-party source system) is the industry-standard acknowledgment that we don't control Salesforce/HubSpot/Stripe APIs. The last sentence preserves a path to scoped use-case commitments when we actually want to make one.

---

Clause 2 — Service credits

Customer's language:
  "If Customer's first-source sync fails due to Provider connector limitations, Provider will apply service credits for the affected month."

Proposed replacement:
  "Any service credits shall be governed exclusively by the Service Level Agreement attached as Exhibit [X] (the 'SLA'). Provider's obligations under this Agreement do not include service credits, refunds, or other monetary relief for any of the following, each of which is the Customer's responsibility: (i) Customer-side permissions, credentials, source-system configuration, or network issues; (ii) changes to a third-party source system's API, schema, authentication, data, or terms; (iii) Source Connectors not listed in the Connector Documentation as generally available (including beta, preview, or custom Connectors); or (iv) setup mistakes, including misconfigured field mappings, sync schedules, destinations, or transformations. The remedies set forth in the SLA and this Agreement are Customer's sole and exclusive remedies for service availability, performance, or Connector issues."

Why: "First-source sync fails due to Provider connector limitations" is the dangerous phrase — "Provider connector limitations" will be litigated on every failed integration, and "first-source sync" is a single binary event that doesn't map to a monthly credit. Moving credits onto the SLA gives the customer a real, defined credit mechanism (typically uptime-based) without exposing us to per-sync adjudication. The four explicit carveouts mirror how support actually triages today — these are the categories that account for the vast majority of "the connector isn't working" tickets.

---

Clause 3 — Connector support and change control

Customer's language:
  "Provider will maintain support for Customer's selected connectors through the subscription term and will not remove or materially change connector behavior without Customer's written approval."

Proposed replacement:
  "Provider will maintain the Source Connectors listed in the Connector Documentation in accordance with its standard support and deprecation policies. Those policies include: (i) reasonable advance notice — and in any event no less than ninety (90) days — before any generally available Source Connector is deprecated or made unavailable, except in cases of emergency caused by a third-party source system's change, in which case Provider will give notice as soon as reasonably practicable; (ii) reasonable effort to avoid material, backward-incompatible changes to Source Connector behavior, and where unavoidable, to provide notice and migration guidance; and (iii) standard support response and resolution targets per the support plan purchased by Customer, as described in Exhibit [Y]. Provider's right to update, improve, and deprecate Source Connectors is part of the Services and is not contingent on Customer's approval. 'Customer's selected connectors' refers to the Source Connectors Customer has configured in its workspace from time to time in accordance with the Connector Documentation, and is not a fixed list frozen at the start of the subscription term."

Why: The original gives the customer an effective roadmap veto — that's a single-customer precedent we can't carry across the book and that prevents normal product iteration. Replacing it with a published deprecation policy (90 days, emergency exception for source-system changes, migration guidance) preserves a real commitment. The closing sentence rebuts the implicit "frozen list" reading of "Customer's selected connectors" by tying selection to the current Connector Documentation rather than a snapshot at signing. Standard support tier references the support plan the customer actually buys — no invented new obligations.

---

Optional fallback positions if customer pushes back on each clause:

  Clause 1: Accept a narrower use-case warranty only if customer names the specific use cases in a Schedule and we get to scope them in writing.
  Clause 2: Offer one (1) month of platform fee credit if a documented platform defect causes a verified first-source sync failure within the first thirty (30) days of initial Source Connector enablement — narrow, time-bounded, and tied to a platform defect, not customer-side causes. Do not extend to "Connector limitations" generally.
  Clause 3: If customer insists on change approval, narrow it to deprecation of Source Connectors that materially represent the customer's primary production integration (top [3] by sync volume), with 180 days' notice and Provider's right to refuse only if a viable migration path exists. Do not concede approval over behavior changes generally.

Manager Q&A — May 5, 2026

Q1. Should we tell teams "durability over motion" is because the fundraising market is bad?
No. "Durability over motion" is an operating posture — focus, sequencing, evidence over assumption — not a read on the market. Don't translate it into market commentary for teams; that's a leadership frame, not a team frame. If asked, point to how we're actually working: clear owners, narrower bets, decisions grounded in real customer signal. Market context belongs in leadership conversations; teams get the operating picture.

Q2. Are paused roles effectively gone for 2026, or paused until Q2 evidence?
Holds, not gone. Tied to named operating signals (real demand, sustained work that requires the role), not a calendar or a cap. If those signals show up, the role reopens. Frame it as disciplined scoping — we add when the work is real, we hold when it isn't yet — not a freeze or a cut. Don't promise a reopen date; promise the trigger.

Q3. If Evergreen lands over 200 active developers in April, should we describe it internally as expansion proof?
No. April usage landing above 200 is consistent with Growth plan usage mechanics — built-in workspace and connector consumption per the Evergreen std-term — not a bespoke expansion motion. Treat it as a usage milestone, not a commercial narrative. It's also not, on its own, a reason to reopen any held role; reopens are driven by named operating signals, not a single customer's usage line. Usage = product health, not a hiring signal.

Q4. How do we keep teams motivated if we're not opening a Series C process in H1?
Motivation isn't tied to a fundraise calendar — that's an investor frame, not a team frame. What's real for teams: meaningful work, clear owners, shipped outcomes, and evidence we're building something customers depend on. Series C is a board/investor decision and isn't an H1 operating focus; that's deliberate, not a signal of trouble. Keep the conversation on what we're building and the signal it's producing.

Q5. What should managers say if someone asks whether Compass staying internal means it's not working?
Compass being internal is a sequencing choice, not a verdict. Right now it's an internal owner workflow — anonymized internal tracker rows, not a customer product — and we're using it to pressure-test evidence and reject work that's too thin before it reaches a customer surface. Whether it's "working" gets read off usage inside Scaffold first; that bar has to clear before naming or repeatability comes up. Internal is intentional, not a retreat.

Thanks for the revised language. Two structural concerns with this clause as drafted:

**1. It captures failures outside Scaffold's control.**
The clause applies when failure arises from "Customer's source-system configuration, permission changes, or changes to the source system's API." Our standard remedy for a covered failure is commercially reasonable remediation, not service credits. Sidebox rewrite below — kept it generic, attributed the 5-minute window to API v2 verification, made the "samples are illustrative" point load-bearing, and steered the failure-mode sentence away from any defect or sequencing framing.

---

About the `nbf` timestamp in this sample

The earlier version of this sample used a fixed `nbf` value so the claim was easy to read at a glance. Fixed sample timestamps are a common source of confusion: when they're copied into real integrations, the token's effective window slides into the past and requests start failing — even though the same code appeared to "work" while you were reading the tutorial.

A few notes for partners integrating against API v2:

  - Clock skew is tolerated, not unlimited. The API v2 verifier accepts `nbf` values within roughly five minutes of the current time on either side. That's why a stale sample token often keeps working for a while, then suddenly doesn't.
  - Samples are illustrative. Don't copy the literal timestamp from this tutorial into production code. Generate `nbf` from the current time in your signing step (a common pattern is `iat`, or `now` with a small skew buffer) rather than reusing a placeholder value.
  - If you see a `nbf` or timestamp-related error after copying this sample, the most likely cause is the borrowed timestamp rather than a change in the verification behavior. Replace it with a dynamic value and re-test.

Full reference for accepted JWT tolerances is in the API v2 authentication docs.

Subject: 401s on token verification — what we saw in the logs

Hi [name],

Thanks for sending those over. Walking through what we found:

The 401s line up with tokens whose `iat` and `nbf` claims are roughly six minutes ahead of our verifier's clock at the moment of rejection. JWT verifiers reject `nbf` values that are still in the future, with a small leeway window (a few seconds in most libraries); six minutes is well outside that window, so the rejections are consistent with how the spec is implemented on our side.

The pattern fits an issuer-side clock drift. You mentioned an NTP issue during the deploy — if the hosts minting tokens were briefly out of sync, freshly issued tokens would carry future-dated `iat`/`nbf` until NTP caught back up. Once your clocks converged, the failures stopped, which is what we'd expect from a skew event rather than a verifier regression.

If you still see a 401 against a token whose `iat`/`nbf` is within a few seconds of your issuer's wall clock (post-sync), please send:

  the full JWT, or its decoded header + payload (so we can read the claims directly),
  the request ID from the 401 response (it appears in the `X-Request-Id` header and in our access logs),
  the issuer host's clock state at the time — `timedatectl status` on systemd hosts or `ntpq -p` / `chronyc tracking` is fine.

That gives us the input to confirm whether anything on our end is rejecting a token it should have accepted. Until we see that, we're treating this as a clock-skew incident on the issuer side and don't have a code change to make.

Locking NTP on the token-issuing hosts (chrony or ntpd against a stable source, with a tight drift threshold) is the durable fix on your side. Happy to jump on a call if it's easier to walk through.

Leo

Two small notes for when you pass it back:

- The "send us logs for replay defects" framing is gone. The new ask is *behavior vs. documented contract*, with request IDs as the anchor — that keeps Atlas in support-contract clarity, not a quiet reliability lane.
- "Replay defects" implied a known class of platform bugs. Without a confirmed issue, that's an overpromise; the rewrite doesn't invite that framing at all.

If Leo wants a one-line variant for the rotation that doesn't have room for bullets, the load-bearing version is: "Retries are at-least-once — dedupe on `X-Scaffold-Event-Id` and verify the signature. If behavior contradicts the webhook docs, send the request IDs and we'll dig in against the contract."

- "Exactly once" overclaims. Webhook systems deliver at-least-once by default; exactly-once needs persisted dedupe, ack-timeout discipline, no queue replay under failure. Stripe/GitHub frame as at-least-once + idempotency key — that's the durable shape. We likely haven't proved it.
- "Exactly once" + "send logs, we'll investigate a replay defect" puts us on the hook for any duplicate. Safer: at-least-once, use event_id as idempotency key, share request_id if you see a duplicate. Same helpful tone, no SLA trap.

Subject: Re: cursor expired after paused sync — recovery path

Hi [name],

Thanks for the detail — the timeline you walked through (cursor cached roughly 36 hours during a paused sync, then a cursor-expired response on resume) lines up with what the API contract says: cursors are short-lived and tied to an active list operation, not to a paused or offline client. That part is behaving as documented.

The clean recovery, once a pause has outlasted the cursor's lifetime, is to discard the cached cursor and restart the list from your last durable object boundary — typically the highest object ID or most recent timestamp you've already successfully written — and let the next page request issue a fresh cursor. Resuming with the expired cursor is what's producing the error; it isn't a defect signal or a data-loss condition. Nothing in your data was missed, the server just won't honor a cursor from a list operation that has aged out.

A couple of connector-side notes that usually make this less surprising next time:

  - After a pause longer than a few minutes, treat any cached cursor as advisory. The signal to discard it should be the pause gap, not the error response.
  - If your sync key is a monotonic field like updated_at, you can often skip the restart entirely and resume from the last written timestamp — the cursor is only needed when you actually need server-side ordering across pages.
  - Worth wiring the resume logic to the "last successful page boundary" your connector already tracks, so the recovery is automatic.

Happy to walk through this against your connector's structure if you want to send the relevant code path.

— Leo

Docs replacement (drop into the API v2 pagination page, replacing the current cursor example):

  Pagination cursors

  Cursors are short-lived. They identify a position within an active
  pagination session and are not durable across long pauses, source
  re-syncs, or extended gaps between requests.

  If pagination is interrupted or paused past the cursor's validity
  window, resume from the last record you successfully processed:

    GET /v2/sources/{id}/records?starting_after=<last_record_id>

  Use the record's stable `id`, not the expired cursor. A cursor issued
  before a long pause may return an error or silently skip records; in
  either case, restart from the durable object boundary above.

  For continuous syncs, prefer the webhook + cursor handoff in the
  webhooks guide over long-running paginated pulls.

Support macro (for the support team library):

  Cursor expired after a long pause — how to resume

  The cursor you're holding is short-lived and expired after the pause,
  which is expected behavior — cursors aren't designed to be replayed
  across long gaps.

  To resume cleanly:

    1. Identify the last record you successfully processed from the
       prior run (use its stable `id`, not the pagination cursor).
    2. Restart pagination from the boundary after that record:
         GET /v2/sources/{id}/records?starting_after=<last_record_id>
    3. Discard the expired cursor.

  Same pattern for webhooks paused past their cursor window — re-sync
  from the last durable boundary rather than replaying the old cursor.

  If you're hitting this on every sync (not just after a long pause),
  send the source ID, the last successful record ID, and the gap
  duration and we'll take a closer look.

Hi [Acme contact],

Thanks for the note on the 429s during the batch metadata sync — those are the standard rate-limit responses, not a stability signal. A few practical details that should help:

1.  What the headers are telling you. Every API v2 response carries:
    -  X-RateLimit-Limit — your budget for the current window
    -  X-RateLimit-Remaining — what's left in the window
    -  X-RateLimit-Reset — when the window resets (Unix seconds)
    On a 429 specifically you'll also see Retry-After, which is the cleanest backoff signal.

2.  Backoff that actually works.
    -  On the first 429, honor Retry-After; fall back to X-RateLimit-Reset if Retry-After is absent.
    -  Add jitter (roughly ±10–20%) so concurrent workers don't retry in lockstep.
    -  Cap concurrency rather than retrying harder. For a batch metadata sync, lowering in-flight count usually clears the 429s faster than tightening retry intervals.
    The reset time you saw in the headers is the documented behavior; the API does not retry on your behalf.

3.  When to send a request ID. For a routine 429 that you can explain by your own concurrency, the response is self-describing — no need to loop us in. Please include the X-Request-ID from the response headers when:
    -  you get a 5xx,
    -  you get a 429 at low parallelism with no recent burst, or
    -  you suspect a data-correctness issue.
    Those are the cases where we'll pull logs.

For context: this batch ran at a higher parallelism than your prior syncs, which is what tipped you into the window limit. We don't see any instability, data loss, or regression on the API v2 side.

Hi [name],

Thanks for the report — happy to take a look.

The pattern you're describing — failures clustered around token-lifetime boundaries, mixed with signature mismatches — usually comes down to one of two things on the validating side: clock drift, or a stale JWKS cache after a signing-key rotation. Both are quick to confirm before we dig further.

1) Clock drift on the validating server

JWTs carry `exp` (and often `iat` / `nbf`) claims, and most libraries check those against the local system clock. Even a few minutes of drift is enough to push a token over the edge of validity right at the moment of verification, which produces "token expired" or "token not yet valid" errors that look intermittent. To confirm:
  - Compare the validating host's clock against a known-good source (e.g. time.google.com, pool.ntp.org) using `chrony tracking`, `timedatectl status`, or `w32tm /query /status`.
  - If drift is more than a minute or two, point the host at NTP, let it settle, and re-test.

2) Stale JWKS cache after key rotation

Scaffold rotates Atlas signing keys on a regular cadence. If the validating process caches the JWKS response in memory and either doesn't honor the `Cache-Control` / `max-age` we return, or the worker is long-lived enough that it hasn't refreshed since the last rotation, it'll keep verifying against the previous key. Tokens signed under the current `kid` then fail with "unknown kid" or a signature mismatch. To confirm:
  - Force a fresh JWKS fetch on the validating service and re-run a failing request. If it succeeds, the cache TTL is the cause.
  - Confirm the `kid` on a failing token matches the `kid` currently published at our `/.well-known/jwks.json`.
  - Make sure the JWKS client respects `Cache-Control`, or set a conservative refresh interval (every 5–10 minutes is typical).

Once both are checked (and corrected if needed), please retry the original flow. In most cases that clears the failures outright.

If you're still seeing JWT verification failures after that, reply with the request IDs (and approximate timestamps) of the failing requests and I'll trace them on our side.

Best,
Leo

Hi — thanks for the report. `cursor_expired_after_24h` is the expected response when a page sequence sits idle longer than the cursor's lifetime; cursors on API v2 are designed for active paging, not durable session state, so a long pause will require a restart.

Recommended pattern:

1. Use the cursor only while the sequence is active. Treat `next_cursor` as a within-sequence token, not persistent state.
2. Persist a durable checkpoint after every successful page — typically the ID (or another stable sort key) of the last object you successfully processed, stored on your side.
3. If you hit `cursor_expired_after_24h`, do not fall back to a from-scratch poll. Resume from the checkpoint by listing with a filter that excludes anything at or below your last processed ID, then continue paginating normally.
4. A "poll everything every minute" loop is not a fix. It is expensive at scale, races against writes, and can still hit the same expiry if any gap between polls exceeds the cursor lifetime.

If you've put the checkpoint + resume pattern in place and still see `cursor_expired_after_24h` firing on a sequence with no long pause and no clock skew worth flagging, reply with the request IDs from the failing calls and we'll dig in — that's the only signal that needs the logs.

— Sarah, API Support


— Internal-example wording (for Leo's cursor-pagination section)

Example — paging /v2/objects with a durable checkpoint

Goal: walk the full collection exactly once, survive process restarts and `cursor_expired_after_24h`, and resume without duplicating or dropping objects.

Pattern (cursor + checkpoint + resume):

1. Page with the cursor while the sequence is active.
   GET /v2/objects?limit=500&cursor=<opaque>
   Each response carries `next_cursor` (or null at end). Treat the cursor as a within-sequence token, not persistent state.

2. Persist a checkpoint after every successful page.
   In your own durable store, keyed by resource type, record:
   - last_processed_id — the highest object ID successfully consumed from the most recent page (or another stable sort key the API returns)
   - optionally: last_page_observed_at, for your own observability
   The checkpoint is the source of truth for "where to resume." The cursor is not.

3. Resume from the checkpoint when the sequence is interrupted.
   One rule, three cases:
   - Process restart mid-sequence: re-read the last page using the same cursor if it is still recent; otherwise fall through to the rule below.
   - Cursor returns `cursor_expired_after_24h` (or you anticipate it will, because the pause exceeded the cursor lifetime): do not start a fresh full poll. Resume by listing with a `since_id=<last_processed_id>` filter (or equivalent server-side filter) until caught up, then continue paginating normally.
   - The sequence has been idle long enough that even the resume query would itself exceed the cursor lifetime: same rule — anchor on the checkpoint, not the cursor.

This example deliberately does not recommend:

- Replacing cursors with a "poll everything every minute" loop. It does not avoid expiry (gaps between polls can still exceed the cursor lifetime), it duplicates work, and it races with writes.
- Treating `cursor_expired_after_24h` as a defect signal in the absence of a recent active page. The cursor lifetime is a documented limit, not a bug.

When to escalate to API support with request IDs:

- After the checkpoint + resume pattern is in place, if `cursor_expired_after_24h` still fires on a sequence with no long pause and no clock skew worth flagging, send the request IDs from the failing calls. That is the only signal the on-call side needs to investigate further.

Draft reply (preserves Leo's 8/4 cursor contract: durable checkpoints, no fresh-poll default, req IDs for escalation):

  Thanks for the detailed writeup — it's helpful to see exactly how the worker moved through the run.

  On the contract question:

  - Cursors are designed to traverse a result set. They are durable checkpoints, intended for exactly the kind of resume your worker needed after the crash — picking up where you left off rather than starting over. The cursor itself didn't go stale; that's what the contract guarantees against.

  - A fresh poll with `created_after` is a separate query mode. It returns every event created since that timestamp, independent of any prior cursor state. The two paths don't coordinate, so when you switch from cursor traversal to fresh polling mid-run, the union of what each returns can overlap. That's expected behavior, not a defect.

  - The practical pattern for nightly exports is to pick one mode per run. Cursor traversal is the right fit when you need resumability across a long worker lifecycle. On the consumer side, deduplicate by event ID — that's the stable identity for an event regardless of which mode returned it.

  If you observe behavior that diverges from this — duplicates inside a single uninterrupted cursor run, missing events under cursor-only traversal, or a cursor that fails to resume — send the request IDs from those calls and we'll investigate. The three you cited (req_cur_4418, req_cur_4419, req_cur_4420) confirm the cursor pages came back successfully from our side; nothing in the request log suggests the run diverged from the documented contract.

Notes for your review:
  - Frames the duplicate risk as a mode-switch choice, not a cursor defect — keeps the customer from concluding the API "dropped" or "doubled" anything on its own.
  - Names event ID as the dedupe key (not request ID), since event ID is the stable identity across modes; request IDs stay scoped to escalation.
  - Does not promise exactly-once across modes, does not open a reliability-roadmap line, does not commit to changes to the cursor contract.
  - Confirms the three req IDs in the customer's own note as the evidence base, so Sarah can close the loop without a second round-trip unless new IDs come in.

Subject: Re: Acme API v2 export — duplicate event IDs after cursor + poll restart

Hi Acme team,

Thanks for the detail on what you saw after the maintenance restart. I pulled the request IDs you mentioned (req_acme_cur_5521, req_acme_cur_5522, req_acme_poll_1189) and walked through them on our side. Both cursor pages completed successfully before the pause, the fresh poll behaved per the v2 contract, and I don't see a server error, data loss, or product defect in any of the three calls.

What you're observing is the expected behavior when cursor traversal and a fresh `created_after` poll are run against the same backing store. Both methods read from the same events table, so any event that lands in the overlap window — between the last cursor page's high-water mark and the poll's start timestamp — will be returned by both. After a pause, restarting with `created_after` set to the last cursor page's end reliably picks those records up a second time, which matches the duplicate IDs you flagged.

This is expected, not a defect, and the standard fix is consumer-side idempotency keyed on event ID:

  - Maintain a set (or equivalent dedupe structure) of event IDs you've already processed.
  - On every poll/page response, drop any event whose ID is already in that set before acting on it.
  - The event ID is stable across cursor and poll responses, so a single dedupe set works across both retrieval paths.

As belt-and-suspenders, you can also set `created_after` strictly later than the `occurred_at` of the last record the cursor returned. But the dedupe step is the durable part — it also covers retries, network blips, and future overlap windows, not just this one scenario.

If you see behavior that doesn't fit this shape — duplicates where the IDs are *not* in the cursor/poll overlap, missing events relative to what the v2 contract says a page should return, or 5xx/server errors on otherwise-valid requests — send us the request IDs and we'll dig into the matching log entries on our side. Anything inside the "expected overlap duplicates" pattern doesn't need a contract change; the dedupe approach above is the right path.

Happy to jump on a quick call if it'd help to walk through the dedupe structure against your current ingest code.

Thanks,
Sarah

Subject: Re: Webhook delivery — req_wh_9041, req_wh_9042, req_wh_9043

Hi [customer name],

Thanks for flagging this and for sending the request IDs. I went through the case with our platform team and wanted to share what we found and how to handle it on your side.

What happened

Your endpoint returned a 502 on the first delivery attempt, which triggered our standard retry. The retry succeeded, and you saw the same event twice. That's working as designed — not a defect.

Our delivery model: at-least-once

Webhook delivery in API v2 is at-least-once, not exactly-once. We retry on any non-2xx response from your endpoint, which means a transient failure (502, timeout, deploy in flight, network blip) will produce a duplicate on the next attempt. We can't promise exactly-once delivery because we can't reliably distinguish "your endpoint rejected the payload" from "your endpoint accepted but the response was lost in transit" — and we won't silently drop events in that ambiguity. This is documented in the API v2 webhook section.

How to dedupe on your side

Every webhook payload includes a stable event ID in `payload.event.id` (and surfaced as the `event_id` header). That ID is identical across every retry of the same event. Treat it as your idempotency key: persist the IDs you've already processed and skip any incoming event whose ID you've seen. That gives you effective exactly-once behavior without depending on our delivery to be exactly-once. For the event you saw twice, both deliveries carried the same event ID.

When to send us request IDs

You don't need to loop us in for routine retries you can dedupe via event ID — that's expected. Please send request IDs when:

  - An event arrives whose event ID doesn't correspond to anything you should have received (unexpected payload).
  - You returned 2xx for an event that never appears in your logs (suspected loss).
  - The same event is delivered many more times than the retry schedule in our docs would produce (something other than normal retry is happening).

In any of those, send the request IDs in the format you already used, plus the event ID and approximate timestamps.

For this case

I reviewed req_wh_9041, req_wh_9042, and req_wh_9043 with engineering. The retry matched our contract, the payload event ID was stable across both deliveries, and we see no delivery defect or data-loss evidence on our side. The expected action on your end is idempotency-by-event-ID, which you've already confirmed is in your handler.

Happy to walk through any of this further — a quick call if helpful, or async on the thread. Let me know.

Best,
Sarah
